findings.reason: the control's failure signature is the one thing a node checks its test against, so a signature the base arm cannot produce either sends the node hunting a wiring fault in a correct test or invites it to weaken the assertion until something else fails.
findings.text: §28's negative control says the base arm must fail "with slots offered because the served ratio reads 0.273", but the section's own arithmetic for that record yields the opposite: 0.273 is 12/44, so capacity reads as the live count and the slots read 0, as the same section states one paragraph earlier; a worker building the test would find slots already 0 at base and could not reproduce the refusal the control names

findings.reason: the section's stated cause and its stated effect point at different mechanisms — a circular ratio, and an unbounded launch path — so a node given only this paragraph cannot tell which of them its change is supposed to move.
findings.text: §28's evidence paragraph claims the served ratio "never sheds" and that "only the 30 s p90 wait bound closes the gate, and a backlog of 20 short waits stays under it", while the same paragraph reports the slots reading 0 with 37 to 44 workers launched for a 0.273 ratio over a 12-wide gate; a ratio equal to width/live makes capacity equal the live count, which sheds every slot, so either the wait bound was below its threshold and the gate still read 0 (a second, unnamed closure) or the published 0 had no effect on launches at all — leaving the mechanism the fix must address unidentified

findings.reason: the cap is the only bound that acts on the launches the section reports, so it is a separate change from the ratio and cannot be closed, reviewed or reverted on the ratio's verdict.
findings.text: §28 is headed "Worker slots are sized by demand, and live workers stay within twice the gate" and delivers two independently testable behaviours: a demand-weighted slot computation with a published demand ratio, and a hard cap of twice the gate width that binds whatever the ratio says (its own third case tests the cap alone)

findings.reason: an uncovered deliverable lets a node pass its gate with the ready count fixed and the worker split absent, and leaves the split unreviewed until a later round.
findings.text: §29's deliverable adds "Workers are split into those with a request in service or at the gate and those running tools", a change to the workers count that is independent of the ready count, and the section's "Done when" has no case for it
